books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, July 5, 1852

stimulus.source_note: Frederick Douglass, “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”, Rochester, New York, July 5, 1852. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me. . . . What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July? I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Douglass’s contrast between “you” and “me” most directly shows that he

options.text: believed the Fourth of July should no longer be celebrated.
options.misconception: Douglass asks what the day means to the enslaved, not that Americans stop marking it; his point is the gap between promise and practice.

options.text: thought enslaved people had no interest in American ideals.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Douglass’s speech holds enslaved people up to the Declaration’s promises; he claims those ideals, he does not dismiss them.

options.text: measured American freedom against the experience of the enslaved.
argued that the Constitution protected slavery forever.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Douglass later read the Constitution as an antislavery document; here he judges the nation’s practice, not the Constitution’s text.

rationales.A: Douglass asks what the day means to the enslaved, not that Americans stop marking it; his point is the gap between promise and practice.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Douglass’s speech holds enslaved people up to the Declaration’s promises; he claims those ideals, he does not dismiss them.
rationales.C: The “you” enjoys life and healing while the “me” endures stripes and death, so Douglass is testing the nation’s freedom by what it feels like to the enslaved.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Douglass later read the Constitution as an antislavery document; here he judges the nation’s practice, not the Constitution’s text.
rationales.general:
1. Split the sentence in two: sunlight brings healing to “you” and stripes and death to “me.”
2. Ask what the split measures: the same Fourth of July means opposite things to the free and the enslaved.
3. Name the move: Douglass judges American freedom by the people it leaves out.
Remember: when a speaker splits “you” from “me,” ask whose experience is being used as the measure.
